title: Verifying an Email Address Without Sending One
summary: See how browser email verification proves mailbox control without sending a message, with form setup, a five-step Node.js token verifier, and trial limitations.
body_markdown:
The Email Verification Protocol lets a site confirm that a user controls an email address without sending an email: the browser gets a signed token from the user’s email provider and submits it with the form.


Most signup flows still say “check your inbox,” and some of the people who switch tabs to find the code never come back. Chrome is testing a replacement. The[Chrome origin trial announced on 8 July 2026](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/email-verification-protocol-origin-trial) began in Chrome 150, and Chrome published an[August 2026 update](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/email-verification-august-2026) afterwards. The protocol itself is defined in the IETF Internet-Draft[draft-hardt-email-verification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-hardt-email-verification/) .


This is not SMTP or MX list cleaning. Those tools check whether a mailbox exists. This protocol proves that the person filling in the form is signed in to that mailbox. The sections below cover the three-party model, the form markup, a complete Node.js verifier split into five steps, and how far you can rely on it during the trial.


## Key Takeaways


- The Email Verification Protocol returns an SD-JWT with key binding: an Email Verification Token signed by the issuer, then a tilde, then a key-binding JWT signed by the browser.
- The browser sits between your site and the email provider, so the provider issues the token without learning which site asked for it.
- A valid token proves an active session with the email provider for that address. It does not prove that mail sent to the address will be delivered.
- The feature is a proposal in a Chrome origin trial that has traffic limits and no end date in Chrome’s posts. In their IETF 126 slides, the draft’s authors (not Chrome) estimated three to six months. Chrome’s documentation names only Gmail as a participating provider.
- If the hidden token field arrives empty, or any verification step fails, send your usual confirmation email.


## What Does Browser Email Verification Replace?


Browser email verification replaces the one-time code or magic-link email that sends users away from your site. The IETF draft walks through what the code flow asks of a user: leave for the mail app, wait for delivery, maybe dig through spam, copy the code, then return and paste it. The draft adds that plenty of people drop out partway. A magic link saves the copy-and-paste step, but the user still has to go to the inbox and wait for the message.


Social login skips the email altogether. The draft notes what that costs: the user has to hold an account with that provider, and you have to build one integration per provider. The Email Verification Protocol uses the same principle (the provider vouches for the address) but works through the browser, with no provider-specific SDK on your site.


## How the Email Verification Protocol Works: Three Parties


The Email Verification Protocol involves three parties. Your site is the verifier (the relying party). The browser sits between you and the issuer, which is the service that runs the user’s email account. Because every exchange passes through the browser, the issuer never finds out which site asked for the token.


```text
Verifier (your site) <--> Browser <--> Issuer (e.g. accounts.google.com)
nonce, validation      binds token      checks session,
to your origin   signs EVT
```


The email provider and the issuer can be different hosts. In Chrome’s example, the provider is gmail.com and the issuer is accounts.google.com.


On the issuer side, the email domain publishes a DNS TXT record that delegates to the issuer. The issuer serves` /.well-known/email-verification` metadata, reports login state to the browser through the Login Status API, and, before signing anything, checks the user’s existing first-party session cookies (see[Secure Cookies and HttpOnly](https://blog.openreplay.com/secure-cookies-and-httponly-attributes-for-security/) for how those cookies should be configured). The draft also lets the browser request per-site private addresses, which the EVT marks with` is_private_email: true` . Chrome’s trial documentation does not describe private addresses. Earlier revisions of the draft let an issuer fall back to a WebAuthn challenge when no valid cookie was present, but revision -02 removed that option, so a request without a session now simply fails.


## The Site Side: Form Markup and Nonce


On your side, the form needs two inputs: a normal email field with` autocomplete="email"` , and a hidden field with` autocomplete="email-verification-token"` that carries a nonce bound to the user’s session. When the form is submitted, the browser fills the hidden field with the token. This is the markup from Chrome’s post, with the nonce rendered by the server:


```text
<  input
name  =  "  email-address  "
type  =  "  email  "
autocomplete  =  "  email  "  >
<  input
type  =  "  hidden  "
name  =  "  token  "
nonce  =  "  rAnD0m-VaLuE  "
autocomplete  =  "  email-verification-token  "  >
```


The draft’s session-binding rules call for a random nonce carrying at least 128 bits of entropy. Generate a fresh one for every verification request and let it expire after a short time. Store the render time next to it, because step 2 of the verifier needs it:


```text
import   {   randomBytes   }   from   "  node:crypto  "  ;


const   nonce   =   randomBytes  (  32  ).  toString  (  "  base64url  "  );   // 256 bits
req  .  session  .  evp   =   {   nonce  ,   renderedAt  :   Date  .  now  ()   };
```


The page also needs your origin trial token. Chrome’s[origin trials documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/origin-trials) explains how to supply it. Per the August update, third-party origin trials are not supported for this feature.


## Verifying the Token on the Server


Server-side verification of an Email Verification Protocol token takes five steps: parse it, check the expected values, check the key binding, check DNS delegation, and verify the issuer’s signature. The form value is` <EVT>~<KB-JWT>` . The EVT is the issuer-signed token and holds` email` ,` email_verified` ,` iss` ,` iat` and a` cnf.jwk` browser key. The KB-JWT is signed by the browser and holds` aud` ,` nonce` ,` iat` and` sd_hash` . Do not trust any decoded claim until every step below has passed. The code uses[jose](https://github.com/panva/jose) and Node built-ins. Each block runs inside a` try` block in one` verifyEmailToken()` function that returns` false` if anything throws.


These are the imports the five steps need:


```text
import   {   createHash   }   from   "  node:crypto  "  ;
import   {   resolveTxt   }   from   "  node:dns/promises  "  ;
import   {
createRemoteJWKSet  ,
decodeJwt  ,
decodeProtectedHeader  ,
importJWK  ,
jwtVerify  ,
}   from   "  jose  "  ;
```


**1. Parse.** Split the value at the tilde and check the` typ` headers.


```text
const   [  evt  ,   kb  ,   ...  rest  ]   =   token  .  split  (  "  ~  "  );
if (  !  evt   ||   !  kb   ||   rest  .  length  )   return   false  ;
const   evtHeader   =   decodeProtectedHeader  (  evt  );
const   kbHeader   =   decodeProtectedHeader  (  kb  );
if (  evtHeader  .  typ   !==   "  evt+jwt  "   ||   kbHeader  .  typ   !==   "  kb+jwt  "  )   return   false  ;
const   evtClaims   =   decodeJwt  (  evt  );
const   kbClaims   =   decodeJwt  (  kb  );
```


Today’s tokens carry no selective disclosures, so the value splits cleanly into two parts. The August update calls this shortcut fragile, because it would break if disclosures were ever added. Chrome recommends parsing the token with an SD-JWT library such as` @sd-jwt/core` , which its own demo now uses.


**2. Expected values.** Chrome’s validation steps check` email_verified` ,` email` ,` nonce` ,` aud` , and an` iat` that falls after the form was rendered. Compare the email case-insensitively: the August update warns that providers may send back the address with different capitalisation from what the user entered.


```text
const   {   nonce  ,   renderedAt   }   =   req  .  session  .  evp   ??   {};
delete   req  .  session  .  evp  ;   // single use
if (  evtClaims  .  email_verified   !==   true  )   return   false  ;
if (  String  (  evtClaims  .  email  ).  toLowerCase  ()   !==   submittedEmail  .  toLowerCase  ())   return   false  ;
if (  !  nonce   ||   kbClaims  .  nonce   !==   nonce  )   return   false  ;
if (  kbClaims  .  aud   !==   "  https://example.com  "  )   return   false  ;
if (  kbClaims  .  iat   <   Math  .  floor  (  renderedAt   /   1000  ))   return   false  ;
// Any maximum age is your own policy; the sources define none.
```


**3. Key binding.**` sd_hash` is the SHA-256 of the EVT including its trailing` ~` . The KB-JWT must also verify against the key in` cnf.jwk` .


```text
const   hash   =   createHash  (  "  sha256  "  ).  update  (  evt   +   "  ~  "  ).  digest  (  "  base64url  "  );
if (  hash   !==   kbClaims  .  sd_hash  )   return   false  ;
const   holderKey   =   await   importJWK  (  evtClaims  .  cnf  .  jwk  ,   kbHeader  .  alg  );
await   jwtVerify  (  kb  ,   holderKey  , {   typ  :   "  kb+jwt  "   });
```


**4. DNS delegation.** Query` _email-verification.<domain>` . The draft requires exactly one TXT record, and its value must begin with` iss=` . Use` dig +short TXT _email-verification.gmail.com` to check a domain by hand.


```text
const   domain   =   submittedEmail  .  split  (  "  @  "  ).  pop  ().  toLowerCase  ();
const   records   =   (  await   resolveTxt  (  `  _email-verification.  ${  domain  }`  ))
.  map  ((  chunks  )   =>   chunks  .  join  (  ""  ));
if (  records  .  length   !==   1   ||   !  records  [  0  ].  startsWith  (  "  iss=  "  ))   return   false  ;
const   issuer   =   records  [  0  ].  slice  (  4  );
```


**5. Discovery and EVT signature.** Fetch the issuer metadata, then verify the EVT against its` jwks_uri` . The draft defines the issuer identifier as` https://` followed by the host from the DNS record, and the EVT’s` iss` claim must match it exactly.


```text
const   meta   =   await   (  await   fetch  (  `  https://  ${  issuer  }  /.well-known/email-verification  `  )).  json  ();
const   jwks   =   createRemoteJWKSet  (  new   URL  (  meta  .  jwks_uri  ));
const   {   payload   }   =   await   jwtVerify  (  evt  ,   jwks  , {
algorithms  :   meta  .  signing_alg_values_supported  ,
typ  :   "  evt+jwt  "  ,
});   // written so it does not depend on a kid header
// The draft's issuer identifier is "https://" plus the DNS host, compared byte for byte.
if (  payload  .  iss   !==   `  https://  ${  issuer  }`  )   return   false  ;
return   true  ;
```


Check Artifact On failure


Parse` ~` split,` typ` headers Send confirmation email


Expected values` email_verified` ,` email` ,` nonce` ,` aud` ,` iat` Send confirmation email


Key binding` sd_hash` , KB-JWT signature vs` cnf.jwk` Send confirmation email


DNS single` iss=` TXT record Send confirmation email


Issuer signature metadata,` jwks_uri` ,` iss` Send confirmation email


The[Node DNS module](https://nodejs.org/api/dns.html) returns each TXT record as an array of chunks, which is why step 4 joins them.


## What Are the Limits of Browser-Based Email Verification?


A successful Email Verification Protocol check shows that the user is currently signed in to their email provider with that address. It says nothing about whether mail you send there will arrive. Chrome and the draft both make this point, so keep sending welcome emails.


The browser profile the user fills the form in must already hold a signed-in session with the provider, and the first time an address is verified the user sees a permission prompt, once per address. In the July release the address had to come from autofill. According to the August update, typing or pasting the address now triggers verification when the field loses focus. The draft also points out a small privacy leak: whether a token arrives tells your site if the user is signed in to the issuer.


## What to Do Now


The Email Verification Protocol is not ready to replace your confirmation email yet. The browser API is incubating at[WICG](https://github.com/WICG/email-verification) , and the protocol is an individual Internet-Draft (revision -02, August 2026). Chrome caps traffic in the trial so that sites don’t build on the feature before it launches. Chrome’s posts give no end date. The estimate of three to six months comes from the draft’s authors, in their[IETF 126 DISPATCH slides](https://datatracker.ietf.org/meeting/126/materials/slides-126-dispatch-email-verification-protocol-evp-01) , not from Chrome. Chrome also warns of backwards-incompatible changes, and the August update says the feature is desktop-only up to Chrome 152, with Android support still being explored. Chrome’s documentation names only Gmail as a participating provider. The draft also lists Hellō as an implementing issuer and mentions a Microsoft Edge origin trial.


Issuance has already changed once. The July post described a form-encoded` request_token` JWT. The draft replaces it with[HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9421) and marks the old format as deprecated. From Chrome 153, Chrome sends` application/json` with` Signature` ,` Signature-Input` and` Signature-Key` headers, and a body that holds only the email address. This is an issuer-side change, and your verifier code is not affected.


Keep your OTP or magic-link flow as the default path. If you join the trial, treat the token as progressive enhancement: when it verifies, skip the email. After verification, create your session the way you normally do (see[Cookies vs localStorage for JWT Auth](https://blog.openreplay.com/cookies-vs-localstorage-jwt-auth/) ). The EVT+KB is a one-time proof and should not be used as a session token.


The protocol replaces “go check your inbox” with a signature check you run on your own server, and the verifier needs only five steps. Add the hidden input and the nonce, deploy` verifyEmailToken()` behind your existing confirmation email, and read the Chrome update post for changes before each Chrome release.


## FAQs


How is the Email Verification Protocol different from Sign in with Google?


Sign in with Google is a per-provider login integration that creates an identity relationship between your site and Google. The Email Verification Protocol only confirms that the user controls an email address. It needs no provider SDK on your site, and because the browser mediates the exchange, the issuer signs the token without learning which site requested it.


Can I use crypto.randomUUID() to generate the nonce?


No. A version 4 UUID contains only 122 random bits, because the version and variant fields take up the remaining 6 bits. The IETF draft requires a nonce with at least 128 bits of entropy. Use randomBytes(32).toString('base64url') from node:crypto instead, which gives 256 bits. Store the nonce in the server session and delete it after one use.


Does the Email Verification Protocol work for addresses on custom domains or providers other than Gmail?


Only if the email domain publishes exactly one _email-verification TXT record, starting with iss=, that delegates to an issuer supporting the protocol. Chrome's documentation names Gmail as the participating email provider. For any other domain without that record, the browser cannot obtain a token, so your verifier should treat it as a failed check and send the normal confirmation email.
